topics.topic: Definition, exposure, permissions, and path-trap treatment of own_proc
questions: What exactly is `own_proc`: a private procfs mount, some process metadata unavailable to user code, or another resource; where is it exposed, with what permissions, and is access to it exempt from the audit hook that traps paths outside the runtime and exchange directory?

What exactly is own_proc: whether and where a private proc filesystem is mounted, which entries and access modes it exposes, and whether accesses to it are permitted or must trigger the outside-path trap?

What exactly is own_proc: must a private procfs be mounted, where is it mounted, which entries or metadata may agent code inspect, and how does that access coexist with the rule that the environment holds only the runtime and exchange-directory mounts and that paths outside them are trapped?

judgement.why: This is the same question about own_proc provisioning, visibility, and path-rule treatment already decided by P3, and the relevant texts have not changed since that judgement.

precedent.topic: Definition, provisioning, visibility, and path-rule treatment of own_proc
quotes: execute_function: [SECURITY_BOUNDARY] MUST start bubblewrap with new user, PID, IPC, UTS and network namespaces and no network interface but the new namespace's own loopback, which bubblewrap brings up, with no capability option, the environment cleared and then set exactly to the imported SANDBOX_ENVIRONMENT constant, exactly the host paths of the imported SANDBOX_RUNTIME_PATHS constant bound read-only, inside the new root the symbolic links of the imported SANDBOX_ROOT_SYMLINKS constant (each name linking to its target, made by bubblewrap --symlink), one fresh private exchange directory bound read-write, bubblewrap's own fresh proc mounted at the imported SANDBOX_PROC_MOUNT constant and minimal dev mounts, and no other host directory; the child dies with its parent, and the runner is the init of the new PID namespace (bubblewrap --as-pid-1), so bubblewrap exits only after the host kernel has killed and reaped every other process of that namespace.

The place is now `SANDBOX_PROC_MOUNT` in the data provider
    (`/proc`): `execute_function` mounts the proc there, `runner_arguments`
    passes it as the member `proc_directory`, and the runner lists it.
precedent.why: The later texts require bubblewrap's fresh private proc filesystem to be mounted at `/proc`.

topics.topic: Meaning and verifiability of the condition that an implementation obtains neither time nor chance
questions: What precisely counts as a function obtaining time or chance, and how can later modules or tests decide whether the qualification applies when the text expressly says alternative sources are not detected? Does the phrase cover only clock and random APIs, or every varying process fact such as object addresses, process accounting, scheduling observations and procfs data?

Does the sandbox have to eliminate every other source of varying observable state, or is equal output promised only for a narrower, unstated class of implementations beyond obtaining no time and no chance?

Is obtains neither a property of the implementation, of one execution path, or of a pair/history of executions, and how can later modules or conformance tests determine that the condition holds when indirect acquisition of time or chance is expressly not detected?

What counts as obtaining time or chance, and how can this condition be established? In particular, do process identifiers, address-dependent values, proc metadata, scheduling observations, filesystem metadata, and other ambient per-execution differences count as chance even though they use none of the trapped entry points?

quotes:
The standard library's own entry points for the clock and for
randomness raise in a function, so it cannot depend on the time or on chance by
accident; code written to get time or chance some other way is not detected and is
judged by its outputs like any other.

Every promise in these documents that a function
repeats itself — equal outputs on equal inputs, a repaired slot staying repaired, a
verdict that holds — is a promise about code that obtains neither.

The list is closed for
   the release; an entry point found missing is added by a new release.

6. An implementation that obtains no time and no chance yields the same output
   digest twice on the same input.

3. Restarting the kernel during a function execution executes it again, with the
   same output digest when it obtains no time and no chance; during an effect it yields `unknown` and no second request.
judgement.divergence: One implementer treats ambient per-execution facts such as addresses, process identifiers, CPU topology and proc metadata as outside “time or chance,” exposes them, and may return different digests for equal inputs; another treats those facts as chance and masks or stabilizes them to preserve equal digests. The agent or caller comparing trial or run outputs notices the difference.
judgement.why: The texts predicate repeatability on obtaining neither time nor chance but neither define that condition nor provide a way to establish it for untrapped ambient observations.

witness.initial: An existing implementation has a conforming value output and returns an integer derived from an ambient per-process fact such as `id(object())`, while calling none of the listed clock or randomness entry points.
events: An agent tries the implementation on a trial case with a fixed input.
The same agent tries the same implementation on the same case again in a fresh sandbox execution.
outcomes: An implementation that treats the ambient fact as outside “chance” exposes the differing fact and records two different output digests.
An implementation that treats every such ambient difference as “chance” masks or stabilizes it and records the same output digest twice.
witness.observer: The agent or caller reading the two TrialExecutions sees equal versus different output digests.
basis:
An implementation is a Python module that defines a top-level function `run`
   taking one argument, a dict with one entry per input port, and returning a dict
   with exactly one entry per output port.

Trying an implementation (State 0 action), by any agent,
   executes an existing implementation on the cases of its contract version's
   corpus that the request names, all of them when it names none, in corpus
   order, records one TrialExecution per case and returns them.

topics.topic: Required restart behavior after an unfinished execution observes other varying state
questions: When an unfinished function observes varying state other than a clock or randomness, must recovery reproduce the original unrecorded execution's output, or may the re-execution produce a different digest?

quotes:
The standard library's own entry points for the clock and for
randomness raise in a function, so it cannot depend on the time or on chance by
accident; code written to get time or chance some other way is not detected and is
judged by its outputs like any other.

Every promise in these documents that a function
repeats itself — equal outputs on equal inputs, a repaired slot staying repaired, a
verdict that holds — is a promise about code that obtains neither.

3. Restarting the kernel during a function execution executes it again, with the
   same output digest when it obtains no time and no chance; during an effect it yields `unknown` and no second request.
judgement.divergence: One recovery implementation exposes varying non-clock process state and records the value observed by the replacement execution; another classifies that state as chance and constrains it so recovery reproduces the interrupted execution's prospective value. The run owner sees different recovered outputs.
judgement.why: Recovery's same-digest condition depends on the undefined boundary of “time or chance,” so the texts do not decide whether other varying ambient state must be reproduced or may vary.

witness.initial: An active flow contains a function returning `os.cpu_count()`, and its run is interrupted after the function observes a CPU count but before any NodeExecution is recorded.
events: The host's visible CPU topology changes after the interrupted observation.
The kernel restarts and re-executes the function during start-up recovery.
outcomes: Recovery exposes the current CPU topology and records a different output from the value the interrupted execution observed.
Recovery treats CPU topology as chance and constrains or reproduces it so the replacement execution yields the same value the interrupted execution observed.
witness.observer: The run owner reading the recovered output and trace sees the resulting CPU-count value.
basis:
The owner or any agent may start a run of an active version (State 0). The
   starter is recorded and never changes.

topics.topic: Whether admission verdicts remain reusable after untrapped acquisition of time or chance
questions: For an implementation that obtains time or chance through an untrapped route, must an existing verdict still be reused unconditionally, or must admission run again because the new qualification says its verdict is not promised to hold; and, if reuse depends on that condition, how can the kernel determine it?

quotes:
Submitting an implementation — new, or equal to an existing one — runs
   admission unless an AdmissionVerdict M08 for that implementation and the
   current corpus digest already exists, in which case that verdict is used.
judgement.why: A04 unconditionally reuses the existing verdict for the implementation and current corpus digest; it states no exception for detected or undetected acquisition of time or chance.
